theory.what: Alerting notifies NOC staff when network metrics exceed predefined thresholds, enabling proactive issue detection before users are impacted. A well-designed alerting system distinguishes between signal (real problems requiring action) and noise (transient spikes, known events, or informational messages). Thresholds define the boundary between normal and abnormal operation. They typically use multiple levels: Warning (70% of capacity — investigate during business hours), Critical (90% — immediate action required), and Informational (unusual patterns worth noting). Alerting integrates with notification channels (email, Slack, PagerDuty, SMS) and escalation policies (primary on-call → secondary → manager) to ensure the right person is notified at the right time.
theory.why: Without automated alerting, NOC engineers must constantly watch dashboards — which doesn't scale beyond a handful of devices. Human monitoring misses transient events, especially overnight. Automated alerts catch issues immediately, day or night. However, poorly tuned alerting creates 'alert fatigue' — too many false alarms desensitize operators to real emergencies. Studies show that after receiving more than 5 alerts per shift, operators begin ignoring alerts. The goal is to tune thresholds so that every alert represents a genuine issue requiring action. A well-tuned alerting system is the difference between proactive NOC operations and 'the users will tell us when something breaks.'
theory.how: Defining effective thresholds: 1) Collect baseline data for 30+ days to understand normal ranges. 2) Set Warning at 70-80% of max normal, Critical at 85-95%. 3) Configurable per device — a core switch may need tighter thresholds than an access switch. 4) Use conditional logic: 'High CPU for 5 consecutive minutes' (not 30-second spike). 5) Maintenance windows should auto-silence alerts. 6) Suppression rules: if one WAN link fails, don't alert for every device behind it (topology-aware alerting). Common metrics to alert on: interface utilization > 80% sustained; CPU > 90% for 5 minutes; temperature > threshold; BGP session down; OSPF neighbor down; fan/cooling failure; device unreachable (ping loss); CRC errors increasing; packet loss > 0.1%.
theory.when: Set alerts for all critical infrastructure: core switches, distribution switches, WAN routers, firewalls, load balancers, DNS/DHCP servers, and internet circuits. Tune thresholds monthly based on alert history — if an alert never triggers or always triggers during known events, adjust. Create separate thresholds for peak vs off-peak hours. After each P1/P2 incident, review whether alerts would have caught it earlier and add missing alerts.
key_concepts: Threshold levels (Warning/Critical)
Escalation policies
Alert fatigue — too many false alarms reduce effectiveness
Acknowledgment — someone must confirm they're handling the alert
Maintenance windows — suppress alerts during planned work
Correlation — suppress related alerts when root cause is identified
Timers — condition must persist for N minutes before alerting
Notification channels — email, Slack, SMS, PagerDuty, phone
theory.configuration:
# Prometheus alerting rule
groups:
  - name: network
    rules:
      - alert: HighInterfaceUtilization
        expr: rate(ifHCInOctets[5m]) * 8 / interface_speed > 0.8
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "Interface {{ $labels.interface }} on {{ $labels.device }} > 80%"
          description: "Utilization {{ $value | humanize }}bps"

# PagerDuty integration with severity-based routing
# Critical → Notify primary on-call immediately
# Warning → Create ticket, notify during business hours
# Informational → Log only, no notification
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Tuning Down Alert Fatigue**
Situation: Interface utilization alert fires 30+ times per day because a backup window pushes utilization to 85% every night.

Problem: Engineers start ignoring all alerts, including genuine ones.

Solution: Create separate thresholds for backup window (21:00-06:00 → Critical at 95%) vs business hours (Critical at 80%). Add maintenance window schedule to suppress alerts during known backup periods. Result: alerts drop from 30/day to 3/day. Engineers pay attention to remaining alerts.

**Worked Example 2: Implementing Topology-Aware Alerting**
Situation: WAN link to remote office fails. This generates 50 alerts: 1 for the link, plus 49 for each device behind it that becomes unreachable.

Solution: Implement dependency mapping: alerts for devices 'behind' the WAN link are suppressed when the WAN link is down. The NOC sees one alert ('WAN link to Site-42 down') instead of 50. After restoring the link, dependent device alerts automatically clear.

**Worked Example 3: Alert Correlation**
Situation: Core switch CPU spikes from 20% to 95%.

Correlated alerts: The alerting system correlates this with a BGP session flap and an interface CRC error spike. Root cause: faulty SFP module on the uplink causing continuous interrupts. Alert system groups these into a single incident with the probable root cause highlighted.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• Good alerting = signal, not noise. Every alert should require action.
• Use multiple threshold levels (Warning/Critical) with different response SLAs
• Tune thresholds regularly based on historical data — stale thresholds cause alert fatigue
• Implement maintenance windows, suppression rules, and dependency mapping
• Test alerting by simulating failures during non-peak hours
• Review alert effectiveness monthly and after every incident

**Best Practice:** Start with fewer, higher-quality alerts. It's better to miss a minor issue than to cry wolf so often that genuine emergencies are ignored. Aim for <5 actionable alerts per shift per engineer.
troubleshooting: Check alert history in your monitoring tool
Verify threshold values are still appropriate (review quarterly)
Review escalation path for completeness (who gets called if primary doesn't respond)
Test notification delivery by triggering test alerts
During outages: check if alerts fired but were missed due to fatigue

theory.what: Incident management is the structured process for detecting, classifying, triaging, investigating, resolving, and learning from network incidents. A 'major incident' causes significant service degradation or total outage. Incidents are classified by severity (P1-P4), with P1 requiring immediate response (total outage, 15-minute response SLA) and P4 being informational (minor cosmetic issue, next-business-day response). The incident lifecycle: Detection (alert or user report) → Triage (assess severity, assign resources) → Investigation (root cause analysis) → Resolution (implement fix) → Recovery (verify service restored) → Closure (document lessons learned). A formal incident management process ensures consistent handling regardless of which engineer is on shift and prevents the chaos of unstructured 'everyone jump on the problem' firefighting.
theory.why: Without a structured incident management process, every outage is handled differently depending on which engineer is on call. Key risks: 1) Critical incidents don't receive immediate attention (wrong severity classification). 2) Fix attempts fail because there's no rollback plan. 3) Communication is poor — stakeholders don't know what's happening. 4) Post-incident learning is lost. 5) Root cause is never identified, so the same incident recurs. A formal process ensures: consistent response times per severity, clear communication channels, documented investigation trail, and systematic root cause analysis. This directly impacts SLA compliance and mean time to repair (MTTR).
theory.how: Lifecycle: Detection → Classification (P1-P4) → Notification → Investigation → Resolution → Post-mortem. Each incident has an incident manager who coordinates resources and communication. For P1/P2: a dedicated bridge call (or Slack channel) is created immediately. Investigation follows a structured troubleshooting methodology (check monitoring → check recent changes → check affected services → deep dive). Resolution includes implementing the fix, verifying service restoration, and communicating closure to stakeholders. The post-mortem (within 5 business days) documents: timeline, root cause, contributing factors, what went well, what went wrong, and action items to prevent recurrence. Key metrics tracked: MTTR (mean time to repair), MTBF (mean time between failures), SLA compliance, incident volume by severity, and recurring incident patterns.
theory.when: Follow the incident management process for every incident. P1/P2 require immediate response, dedicated incident commander, and mandatory post-mortem. P3 can follow a streamlined process (investigate during business hours, ticket-only documentation). Regular review of incident trends (monthly) identifies recurring issues and areas for improvement.
key_concepts: Severity classification — P1 (total outage) through P4 (informational)
Escalation matrix — who to notify at each severity level
MTTR (Mean Time to Repair) — key performance metric
Post-mortem — structured learning after P1/P2 incidents
Incident commander — single point of control during major incidents
Communication plan — regular updates to stakeholders during incidents
Rollback plan — always have the ability to revert changes
theory.configuration:
# Severity levels
P1: Total outage or critical impact
  Response: Immediate (15 min)

  Response: < 15 minutes

theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: P1 Incident Response**
Situation: Core switch failure at 02:30 takes down a major data center. All 500 servers unreachable.

Timeline:
02:30 — Automated alert: 'Core-SW-01 unreachable' fires.
02:31 — On-call engineer acknowledges via PagerDuty.
02:35 — Engineer joins bridge call. Incident commander assigned.
02:40 — Initial triage: console access down (out-of-band), can't SSH. Physical issue.
02:45 — Data center technician dispatched.
02:50 — Engineer communicates: 'P1 incident, core switch down, DC tech en route for physical inspection.'
03:00 — DC tech confirms: switch powered off — PDU tripped.
03:05 — PDU reset, switch powers on.
03:10 — Switch boots, BGP/OSPF converge.
03:15 — All services restored. Incident commander declares resolution.
03:20 — Initial post-mortem starts: root cause = PDU overloaded (2A overrated). Fix = redistribute load across two PDUs.

Post-mortem action items: add PDU capacity monitoring, distribute core switch power across dual PDUs, implement automated power monitoring alerts.

MTTR: 45 minutes (target: <60 min for P1).

**Worked Example 2: Incident Communication Template**
Initial notification: 'INCIDENT: P1 — Core network down at DC1. All services affected. Estimate: investigating. Next update: 30 min.'
Update 1: 'Root cause identified: Core switch power failure. DC tech on site. Estimate: 15 minutes to restore.'
Resolution: 'All services restored. Root cause: PDU overload. Full post-mortem within 5 business days.'
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• Structured incident management ensures consistent, effective response
• Severity classification (P1-P4) determines response speed and escalation
• Every major incident needs a designated incident commander
• Post-mortems drive continuous improvement — 'blameless' culture
• Track MTTR, MTBF, and incident trends to measure NOC effectiveness
• Communication during incidents is as important as technical resolution
• Always have a rollback plan for any change

**Best Practice:** Run incident simulations quarterly. Document all incident responses to identify improvement areas. Hold blameless post-mortems — focus on system/process fixes, not individual mistakes.
troubleshooting: Check monitoring dashboards for affected systems
Review recent changes (RFCs, config changes, software updates)
Isolate the affected network segment — does the issue follow a device or a topology?
Check if similar incidents have occurred before (knowledge base)
Verify rollback plan before making changes during incident

theory.what: Change management is the formal process for planning, reviewing, approving, scheduling, implementing, and verifying network changes. It's designed to minimize the risk of outages caused by changes while enabling necessary updates to happen efficiently. Changes are categorized by risk: Standard (pre-approved, low risk — e.g., adding a new user VLAN), Normal (requires CAB approval — e.g., adding a new WAN circuit), and Emergency (expedited for security patches or outage fixes — requires post-implementation review). The change management process includes: a detailed implementation plan, rollback procedure, risk assessment, impact analysis, and testing results. A Change Advisory Board (CAB) reviews Normal changes scheduled for each change window.
theory.why: Uncontrolled changes are the #1 cause of network outages. ITIL research shows 80% of outages are caused by changes — either the change itself is wrong, an unintended side effect occurs, or multiple changes interact poorly. Change management prevents these by ensuring: 1) Every change has a detailed plan and rollback. 2) Changes are reviewed by peers who might spot issues the author missed. 3) Changes are scheduled to minimize business impact. 4) Emergency changes are tracked and audited. 5) Post-change verification confirms the change achieved its goal without side effects. Without change management, the network becomes fragile — nobody knows what was changed, when, or why, making troubleshooting impossible.
theory.how: Change process: 1) Request — submit change ticket with detailed plan, risk assessment, rollback procedure, and testing results. 2) Review — CAB (Change Advisory Board) meets weekly to review changes. Standard changes are pre-approved. 3) Schedule — changes are batched into change windows (weekly maintenance windows, e.g., Thursday 02:00-06:00). 4) Implement — one engineer makes the change, another verifies (four-eyes principle). 5) Verify — confirm change achieved desired outcome with no adverse side effects. 6) Close — update ticket with as-built configuration, notify stakeholders. 7) Emergency changes — fast-tracked through emergency CAB, but require post-change review within 48 hours. Every change is logged and auditable.
theory.when: Every network change (any modification to device configuration, software version, cabling, or infrastructure) must go through change management. Exceptions only for: troubleshooting steps during an active incident (but must be documented within 24 hours) and automated changes from approved automation tools (changes still logged but pre-approved).
key_concepts: CAB (Change Advisory Board) — reviews and approves changes
Maintenance window — scheduled time for implementing changes
Rollback plan — how to revert the change if something goes wrong
Risk assessment — impact analysis before implementing
Standard/Normal/Emergency — change types with different approval paths
Four-eyes principle — one implements, one verifies
Post-change verification — confirm change was successful
theory.configuration:
# Change types
Standard: Pre-approved, low risk
  Example: Adding new user VLAN
  Approval: None (pre-approved)
  Timeline: Next maintenance window

Normal: CAB approval required
  Example: OSPF area redesign
  Approval: Weekly CAB meeting
  Timeline: Next window after approval

Emergency: Expedited, post-review
  Example: Security patch for active vulnerability
  Approval: Emergency CAB chair
  Timeline: ASAP
  Post-review: Within 48 hours
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Normal Change Request**
Change: Add new 100 Mbps MPLS circuit between HQ and data center.

Change ticket includes: 1) Implementation plan: order circuit, configure interface, configure BGP peering, add route-maps, test. 2) Rollback plan: shut down new interface, BGP will withdraw routes automatically, remove configs. 3) Risk assessment: LOW — new circuit is additional capacity, no existing services affected. 4) Testing: ping across circuit, verify BGP prefixes received, test failover of backup traffic.

CAB approves. Change implemented during Thursday 02:00 window. Post-change verification shows BGP peering up, routes received correctly, no adverse impact.

**Worked Example 2: Change Gone Wrong — Emergency Rollback**
Change: Modify ACL on border firewall to allow new vendor API access.

Implementation: Engineer adds new ACL rule. Immediately, critical application monitoring alerts show connectivity failures to a third-party service.

Response: Engineer identifies the new ACL rule is being matched before an existing rule (first-match). Immediate rollback: remove the new ACL rule. Service restores within 2 minutes.

Root cause: ACL rule ordering error — new rule was inserted at sequence 5 instead of the correct sequence 105. Fix: re-implement with correct sequence number after testing in lab.

Lesson: Always specify ACL sequence numbers explicitly. Test ACLs before applying to production.

**Worked Example 3: Emergency Change for Security Vulnerability**
Situation: Critical CVE announced for router IOS version (remote code execution). CVE score 9.8/10.

Emergency change: 1) Emergency CAB authorizes immediate upgrade. 2) Engineer upgrades standby device in HA pair (no service impact). 3) Verify standby is operational. 4) Failover active → standby. 5) Upgrade original active. 6) Fail back. 7) Document in emergency change ticket.

MTTR for vulnerability: 4 hours from CVE disclosure to patched fleet.

Without emergency change process: would wait until next weekly maintenance window (3-5 days) — leaving infrastructure exposed.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• Change management prevents 80% of network outages caused by uncontrolled changes
• Every change needs: plan, rollback, risk assessment, and verification
• Standard/Normal/Emergency categories balance speed vs safety
• Four-eyes principle reduces human error during implementation
• Emergency changes must be tracked and audited (but not blocked)
• Post-change verification is mandatory — confirm the change worked and nothing else broke

**Best Practice:** Always implement changes during maintenance windows. Test changes in a lab or staging environment first. Document every change. Review change success/failure rates monthly. If a change requires a rollback, investigate why and improve the process.
troubleshooting: Verify change was successful by testing the affected service
Check for unintended side effects — monitor dashboards after change
Compare before/after configs (use automated config backup tools)
If change caused issues: execute rollback plan immediately
Post-change: document any deviations from the implementation plan

theory.what: Root Cause Analysis (RCA) is a systematic investigation to identify the fundamental cause of an incident — not just the immediate symptom. It answers 'why did this really happen?' so the fix addresses the root cause, not just the symptom. Common RCA methodologies include: 5 Whys (iteratively ask 'why' until the fundamental cause is identified), Fishbone/Ishikawa diagram (categorize potential causes into people, process, equipment, environment), Fault Tree Analysis (deductive approach starting from the failure), and Timeline Analysis (map events chronologically to identify causal relationships). A good RCA identifies contributing factors (conditions that enabled the root cause to occur) and produces specific, actionable recommendations.
theory.why: Fixing symptoms without identifying root cause means problems recur. Example: router crash — restarting it fixes the symptom, but if the root cause is a memory leak from a buggy IOS version, it will crash again. Without RCA: repeated incidents, wasted engineer time, SLA breaches, and reduced stakeholder confidence. With RCA: each incident reduces the probability of similar future incidents. The compounding effect over years is transformative. A culture of blameless RCA (where the goal is to find system/process weaknesses, not assign blame) encourages engineers to report issues honestly, leading to faster, more effective learning.
theory.how: RCA process: 1) Gather all data — logs, metrics, configuration history, change records, incident timeline, interviews. 2) Build timeline — map every event chronologically. 3) Apply methodology — use 5 Whys or Fishbone to drill down from symptom to root cause. 4) Identify contributing factors — conditions that made the root cause possible (e.g., 'No monitoring on that interface' allowed the issue to go undetected). 5) Develop action items — specific, measurable changes to prevent recurrence. 6) Write RCA report — executive summary + technical detail + action items. 7) Track action items to completion. Timeline analysis often reveals that the root cause was a change hours or days earlier, and the actual outage was just the delayed effect.
theory.when: Perform a formal RCA for every P1 and P2 incident. For P3/P4: a lighter analysis is appropriate — document cause and fix, but skip formal report. RCAs should be completed within 5 business days of the incident while details are fresh. Track all action items in a system with owners and due dates.
key_concepts: 5 Whys — simple, iterative questioning
Fishbone/Ishikawa diagram — structured multi-category analysis
Timeline reconstruction — chronological event mapping
Contributing factors — conditions enabling the root cause
Blameless culture — focus on system/process, not individuals
Action items — specific changes to prevent recurrence
Human factors — many RCAs ultimately trace to human error; system design should prevent or catch errors
theory.configuration:
# 5 Whys Example — Core Switch Outage
1. Why did the outage occur?
   Core switch stopped forwarding packets.
2. Why did core switch stop forwarding?
   CPU reached 100% and dropped routing protocol packets.
3. Why was CPU at 100%?
   Continuous STP topology changes consumed CPU.
4. Why were there continuous STP changes?
   An unauthorized switch was connected to an access port.
5. Why was an unauthorized switch allowed?
   No BPDUGuard on access ports and no port security policy.

Root Cause: Unauthorized device connected to an unprotected access port caused STP instability, consuming the core switch CPU.

Action Items:
1. Enable BPDUGuard on all access ports (owner: NOC Lead, due: 2 weeks)
2. Implement port security with MAC limiting (owner: Security Engineer, due: 1 month)
3. Configure BPDUGuard violation = shutdown instead of log (owner: NOC Lead, due: 2 weeks)
4. Audit all access ports quarterly for compliance (owner: NOC Manager, due: ongoing)

Fishbone categories: People (unauthorized device plugged in), Process (no access port hardening policy), Equipment (access port allowed BPDUs), Environment (no physical security preventing unauthorized access).
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example: Complex RCA — Intermittent App Performance**
Symptom: Application performance degrades for 2-3 minutes several times per day.

Timeline analysis:
09:00 — App slow, clears by 09:03
11:30 — App slow, clears by 11:32
14:15 — App slow, clears by 14:18
16:45 — App slow, clears by 16:47

Correlating with network data:
09:00 — WAN utilization spike to 60 Mbps (normal: 20 Mbps)
09:03 — WAN drops back to 20 Mbps

Investigation reveals WAN backup window every 4 hours starting at 09:00, 13:00. Wait — 13:00 doesn't match. Check timezone: backup server is in UTC, NOC is in EST (UTC-5). Backup timer set for 14:00 UTC = 09:00 EST. The backup window collides with business hours.

Root Cause: Backup schedule in UTC not converted to local time. Backup ran during business hours, saturating the WAN link. QoS not configured for backup traffic.

Action Items: 1) Move backup to 20:00 EST (01:00 UTC) — no business impact. 2) Enable QoS to prioritize production traffic over backup, limiting backup to 30% of bandwidth. 3) Add backup scheduling timezone check to change management checklist.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• RCA identifies the fundamental cause of an incident — fix root cause, not symptom
• The 5 Whys is the simplest effective RCA technique for most network incidents
• Always build a timeline before analyzing causes
• Identify contributing factors in addition to root cause
• A blameless culture produces better RCAs — focus on system/process fixes
• Track action items to completion; an RCA without action items is just a report

**Best Practice:** Complete RCAs within 5 business days. Present findings to the team — collective learning prevents recurrence across all engineers. Each RCA should produce 2-3 specific, measurable action items with owners and due dates.
troubleshooting: Gather all available logs, metrics, and configuration archives
Build a detailed timeline of events
Interview everyone involved while memories are fresh
Identify all contributing factors, not just the root cause
Verify action items prevent recurrence — don't just address symptoms

theory.what: Service Level Agreements (SLAs) define measurable targets for network availability, performance, and support response times. They set clear expectations between service providers and customers (internal or external). Common SLA metrics: Availability (uptime percentage — 99.9%, 99.99%, 99.999%), Latency (one-way or round-trip delay), Packet Loss (percentage of packets dropped), Jitter (variation in delay), MTTR (mean time to repair), MTBF (mean time between failures), and Response Time (how quickly the NOC responds to incidents). SLAs often include penalties (service credits) if targets are missed and require regular reporting (monthly SLA reports).
theory.why: SLAs serve multiple purposes: 1) They set clear expectations — everyone agrees what 'good' looks like. 2) They drive investment decisions — achieving 5 nines (99.999%) requires redundant infrastructure, which costs more. 3) They provide a basis for continuous improvement — measuring performance against targets identifies gaps. 4) They protect both provider and customer by defining boundaries. 5) In regulated industries (finance, healthcare), SLAs may be mandated by compliance. Without SLAs, the NOC has no objective measure of success, and customers have no recourse if service is poor.
theory.how: Defining SLAs: 1) Identify critical services (core connectivity, internet, VPN, DNS). 2) Define measurable metrics for each service. 3) Set realistic targets based on current capability (don't promise what you can't deliver). 4) Define measurement methodology (monitoring tool, calculation method, reporting period). 5) Establish penalties/remedies for missed targets. 6) Define escalation process when SLAs are at risk. Common calculation: Availability = uptime / (uptime + downtime) × 100. Exclude planned maintenance from availability calculations (unless specified otherwise). Monthly reporting tracks SLA performance and trends.
theory.when: Define SLAs for all critical services before deploying them. Review SLAs annually to adjust targets as infrastructure improves or business needs change. Monitor SLA compliance continuously — don't wait for monthly reports to discover you're missing targets. When an SLA is breached or at risk, trigger an investigation immediately.
key_concepts: Availability nines — 99.9% (8.76 hr/yr), 99.99% (52.6 min/yr), 99.999% (5.26 min/yr)
MTTR/MTBF — mean time to repair / between failures
Latency targets — usually < 50ms inter-DC, < 150ms intra-continent
Packet loss target — typically < 0.1%
Response time — how fast NOC acknowledges and begins working on incidents
SLA credits — financial penalty for missed targets
Reporting — monthly SLA compliance reports for stakeholders
theory.configuration:
# SLA targets for enterprise WAN
Service: Core Network Connectivity
  Availability: 99.99% (52.6 min/yr downtime max)
  Latency (inter-DC): < 10 ms one-way
  Packet loss: < 0.01%
  MTTR: < 4 hours for P1

Service: Internet Connectivity
  Availability: 99.9%
  Latency (to major sites): < 50 ms
  Packet loss: < 0.1%
  MTTR: < 2 hours for P1

Service: DNS Resolution
  Availability: 99.999%
  Response time: < 10 ms (internal), < 50 ms (external)
  Uptime: Redundant DNS servers

SLA Credits:
  < 99.99% availability: 10% monthly fee credit
  < 99.9% availability: 25% monthly fee credit
  < 99.0% availability: 50% monthly fee credit

Planned maintenance: Not counted against availability (minimum 5 days notice)
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Calculating Availability**
Circuit uptime = 30 days (720 hours).

Scenario A: Unplanned downtime = 1 hour (router crash + reboot).
  Availability = (720 - 1) / 720 × 100 = 99.86%
  SLA target: 99.9%. Breached!

Scenario B: Unplanned downtime = 30 minutes.
  Availability = (720 - 0.5) / 720 × 100 = 99.93%
  Within SLA.

Lesson: With a 99.9% SLA, you have about 43 minutes of downtime per month. One unexpected router crash could breach the entire month's SLA.

**Worked Example 2: SLA Reporting**
Monthly report shows:
- Core network availability: 99.95% (meets 99.99%? No — breached! 43 minutes of allowed downtime exceeded)
- Internet latency: 45 ms average (meets 50 ms target: Yes)
- MTTR P1: 3.5 hours (meets 4-hour target: Yes)
- Packet loss: 0.01% (meets target: Yes)

Breach analysis: The 99.95% availability breach was caused by a 3-hour fiber cut by a third-party contractor. Action item: implement diverse fiber paths for the affected link to eliminate single-point-of-failure.

**Worked Example 3: Using SLAs to Drive Investment**
Current: 99.9% availability for internet connectivity (8.76 hr/yr downtime). Business requirement: e-commerce site needs 99.99% (52 min/yr).

Required investment: Add a second ISP connection (diverse physical path, different carrier). Implement BGP with local-preference for active/standby failover. Estimated cost: $12,000/year. Downtime reduction: from 8.76 hr/yr to ~30 min/yr (well within 52 min target).

ROI: prevented revenue loss during outages vs cost of redundancy.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• SLAs define measurable targets for availability, performance, and response
• 99.9% = 8.76 hr/yr downtime; 99.99% = 52.6 min/yr; 99.999% = 5.26 min/yr
• Always define measurement methodology before setting targets
• Monitor SLA compliance continuously — monthly reports are for stakeholders, not for detection
• Planned maintenance should be excluded from SLA calculations
• Breaches should trigger investigation and corrective action
• SLAs drive investment decisions for redundancy and reliability

**Best Practice:** Set realistic SLAs that you can consistently meet. It's better to set 99.9% and exceed it than to set 99.99% and breach monthly. Review SLAs annually and adjust upward as infrastructure improves. Use SLA breaches to justify investment in redundancy.
troubleshooting: Check SLA dashboard for current compliance status
Review incidents that contributed to downtime
Calculate availability for the current month-to-date
Identify which metrics are at risk of breaching targets
Proactive: escalate when an incident risks SLA breach so management is informed

theory.what: Network documentation is the practice of maintaining accurate, up-to-date records of network topology, device configurations, IP addressing, cabling, and operational procedures. Essential documentation includes: network diagrams (L2/L3 topology, physical cabling, rack elevations), IP Address Management (IPAM — tracking IP assignments), device inventory (model, serial number, software version, location, warranty), configuration backups (automated, version-controlled), standard operating procedures (SOPs — for common tasks), runbooks (incident response procedures), password/credential management, vendor contracts and support entitlements, and circuit/WAN information (carrier, circuit ID, bandwidth, contract dates).
theory.why: Without accurate documentation, every troubleshooting session starts from zero — engineers must discover the network as it exists, which is time-consuming and error-prone. Specific risks: 1) IP address conflicts because IPAM is not updated. 2) Disaster recovery is impossible without topology diagrams. 3) New engineers take months to learn the network. 4) Audit/compliance failures due to incomplete records. 5) Unnecessary outages during maintenance because the impact wasn't documented. Good documentation reduces MTTR significantly — studies show 30-50% faster troubleshooting when documentation is current. Documentation is the 'source of truth' that all operations are based on.
theory.how: Essential documentation types: 1) Network diagrams — L2 topology (STP, VLANs, trunks), L3 topology (IP subnets, routing protocols, BGP AS numbers). Update after every change. 2) IPAM — spreadsheet or tool (NetBox, phpIPAM, SolarWinds IPAM). Track: subnet, VLAN, assignment, purpose, owner, and date. 3) Device inventory — model, serial, software, location, ports, warranty, support contract. 4) Configuration backups — automated via Oxidized/RANCID, stored in Git. 5) SOPs/runbooks — step-by-step for common tasks: 'Adding a new VLAN', 'Responding to BGP flap'. 6) Password/credential vault — privileged access management (CyberArk, HashiCorp Vault). Documentation should be treated as a living system — updated as part of every change and reviewed quarterly for accuracy.
theory.when: Document as you go — update documentation at the same time as you make the change. If documentation becomes stale, schedule a documentation improvement sprint. Review all documentation quarterly. Audit critical documentation (network diagrams, IPAM, device inventory) monthly. For new builds: document during implementation, not after.
key_concepts: Network diagrams (L2/L3 topology)
IPAM (IP Address Management)
Device inventory
Configuration backups (automated, version-controlled)
SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures)
Runbooks (incident response)
Password/credential management
Single source of truth — one authoritative location, not scattered spreadsheets

theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Documentation During an Outage**
Symptom: DNS resolution fails for internal applications.

With good documentation: Engineer checks runbook 'DNS Troubleshooting'. Runbook shows: 1) Check DNS server status (IP 10.0.0.10, 10.0.0.11). 2) Check network connectivity to DNS servers. 3) Check DNS service status. 4) Check DNS zone transfers. 5) Escalation path: DNS admin (name + phone).

Result: DNS restored in 15 minutes. The runbook includes the exact restoration procedure and contact information.

Without documentation: Engineer has to ask colleagues 'who manages DNS?', find server IPs from memory, figure out the test procedure from scratch. Result: DNS restored in 60 minutes.

**Worked Example 2: Keeping Documentation Current**
Strategy: 1) Change management ticket includes a 'Documentation updated' checkbox that must be checked before the change is closed. 2) Automated config backup (Oxidized + Git) captures the actual configuration after every change. 3) Monthly spot-check: automated tool verifies device configs match documentation (NetBox vs actual config). 4) Quarterly 'doc audit': randomly select 5% of documentation items and verify against actual network. 5) When documentation is found to be wrong, it's treated as a bug and fixed.

**Worked Example 3: IPAM Best Practices**
A /16 network (10.0.0.0/16) is divided into documented subnets:
  10.0.0.0/24 — Network infrastructure (routers, switches)
  10.0.10.0/24 — Servers (production)
  10.0.20.0/24 — Servers (staging)
  10.0.30.0/24 — Management network
  10.0.100.0/24 — WiFi users
  ...

Each subnet is documented in NetBox with: VLAN ID, purpose, responsible team, gateway, DHCP scope info. A new engineer can look at NetBox and understand the entire IP scheme in 30 minutes.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• Good documentation reduces MTTR by 30-50%
• Essential: network diagrams, IPAM, device inventory, config backups, runbooks
• Update documentation AS you make changes, not after
• Use tools (NetBox, Oxidized, draw.io) rather than manual spreadsheets
• Quarterly documentation audits prevent drift
• Documentation is a 'source of truth' — only as good as its accuracy
• SOPs and runbooks enable engineer consistency and faster onboarding

**Best Practice:** Treat documentation as critical infrastructure. Automate what you can (config backups, IPAM discovery). Review documentation accuracy quarterly. The question 'is this documented?' should always be answered 'yes' before any change is made.
troubleshooting: Is documentation current? Check last update date on critical docs
Is the network diagram accurate? Verify by tracing a path between two devices
Check IPAM for conflicts before adding new IP addresses
When troubleshooting: check runbooks for the affected system first
Verify config backups are running — automated backup is the safety net

theory.what: Performance baselining establishes the 'normal' operating parameters of a network — the baseline against which all future measurements are compared. Without a baseline, engineers can't distinguish between normal fluctuations and genuine anomalies. Baseline measurements include: interface utilization (average, peak, 95th percentile), CPU/memory usage across devices, latency and jitter between key points, packet loss, error rates, TCP connection counts, DNS resolution times, and application response times. A proper baseline captures data over at least 30 days (one full business cycle) to account for daily and weekly patterns. The 95th percentile is the standard measurement for capacity planning — it excludes the top 5% of spikes, representing the sustained peak load.
theory.why: Without baselines, you can't answer fundamental questions: 'Is this normal?' 'Are we growing?' 'Do we need to upgrade?' Specific benefits: 1) Anomaly detection — sudden deviation from baseline triggers investigation. 2) Capacity planning — growth rate vs baseline shows when capacity will be exhausted. 3) Performance troubleshooting — comparing current to baseline reveals what changed. 4) SLA reporting — baseline data provides evidence of compliance. 5) Investment justification — 'utilization has grown 40% year-over-year' is a strong argument for upgrades. A baseline turns subjective 'the network feels slow' into objective 'latency is 30ms above the 6-month baseline.'
theory.how: Baselining process: 1) Identify what to measure — interface utilization, CPU, latency, errors, etc. 2) Collect data for 30+ days using monitoring tools (SNMP polling, NetFlow, streaming telemetry). 3) Calculate statistics for each metric: average, peak, 95th percentile, standard deviation. 4) Document expected ranges for different times of day and days of week. 5) Set threshold alerts based on baseline + headroom (e.g., alert when utilization > 2× baseline standard deviation). 6) Re-baseline quarterly to capture growth and seasonal patterns. 7) Compare each period's baseline to identify trends. The 95th percentile is especially important: it represents the sustained peak, excluding transient spikes.
theory.when: Establish baselines for all new deployments within 30 days of commissioning. Re-baseline quarterly for critical links. Always take a baseline before making significant changes — if performance degrades after the change, you have evidence. When investigating performance issues, compare current data to the most recent baseline.
key_concepts: 95th percentile — standard capacity planning metric
Average vs Peak vs 95th percentile — each tells a different story
Seasonal patterns — daily, weekly, monthly cycles affect baselines
Anomaly detection — deviation from baseline triggers investigation
Standard deviation — measures how 'normal' the variation is
Growth rate — year-over-year comparison shows trends
Baseline drift — slowly changing normal that may indicate a problem
theory.configuration:
# Key metrics to baseline
Metric: Interface Utilization (In/Out)
  Measurement: bits per second

  Statistics: avg, max, 95th percentile
  Baseline period: 30 days (rolling)
  Alert threshold: > 95th percentile × 1.5 for 15 minutes

Metric: Latency (round-trip)
  Measurement: milliseconds
  Collection: ICMP echo every 60 seconds
  Statistics: avg, min, max, jitter (variance)

Metric: CPU utilization (device)
  Measurement: percentage
  Collection: SNMP polling every 5 minutes
  Statistics: avg, peak
  Alert threshold: > 90% for 10 minutes

Metric: Packet loss
  Measurement: percentage of packets lost
  Collection: ICMP echo every 60 seconds
  Alert threshold: > 0.1% for 5 minutes
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Anomaly Detection**
Baseline: WAN link utilization = 30% average, 65% peak (95th percentile).

Monday 10:00: Utilization suddenly jumps to 92% and stays there.

Anomaly detection: This is 2.5× the normal peak. Automatically triggers investigation. Engineer checks: is it a new backup job? DDoS attack? Traffic shift from another link?

Root cause: A new server backup job was configured to run during business hours. Job moved to off-peak, utilization drops back to baseline.

Without baseline: 'Is 92% bad? I don't know, maybe it's always like this.'

**Worked Example 2: Capacity Planning**
Baseline data collected over 12 months:
  January: 95th percentile = 200 Mbps
  April: 95th percentile = 220 Mbps
  July: 95th percentile = 250 Mbps
  October: 95th percentile = 280 Mbps
  Growth rate: ~40 Mbps / quarter (~80 Mbps / year)

Prediction: Current link is 1 Gbps. At current growth, 95th percentile will hit 1 Gbps in ~7 years. But wait — the growth rate is accelerating (40 Mbps → 50 Mbps → 60 Mbps). Extrapolating: 95th percentile will reach 500 Mbps in 2 years. Plan upgrade to 10 Gbps link, order 6 months before projected exhaustion.

With baseline data: informed decision, right-sizing, cost-effective upgrade timing.
Without baseline: reactive upgrade when link is already saturated and users are complaining.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• Baseline = normal operating parameters, essential for anomaly detection
• Collect 30+ days of data for each metric (one full business cycle)
• Use 95th percentile for capacity planning (sustained peak, excluding transients)
• Re-baseline quarterly to capture growth and seasonal patterns
• Compare current performance to baseline for objective troubleshooting
• Baseline drift may indicate gradual degradation requiring investigation

**Best Practice:** Use rolling 30-day baselines updated weekly. Alert when metrics deviate > 3σ from baseline mean. Review growth trends quarterly. Compare year-over-year baselines for long-term capacity planning. Store baseline data for at least 2 years for trend analysis.
troubleshooting: Compare current metrics to baseline: is this normal or anomalous?
Look for deviations that coincide with other events (changes, time of day)
Check if baseline is outdated — re-baseline after significant network changes
If multiple metrics deviate simultaneously, they may share a root cause
Investigate anomalies immediately — early detection reduces impact

theory.what: Grafana is an open-source visualization platform for creating real-time monitoring dashboards. It connects to multiple data sources (Prometheus, InfluxDB, Elasticsearch, Graphite, CloudWatch, and many more) and visualizes data through panels: time-series graphs, gauges, bar charts, heatmaps, tables, and alert rules. Dashboards are shareable and version-controlled as JSON. Grafana supports variables (dropdown selectors for devices, metrics, time ranges), annotations (mark events on graphs), alerting (with notification channels to Slack, PagerDuty, email), and team collaboration (dashboard comments, sharing). It's the standard visualization layer in modern NOC stacks.
theory.why: Raw metrics in a time-series database tell you nothing visually. Grafana transforms numbers into actionable insights: you can see utilization spikes, correlate events across metrics, spot trends, and understand network behavior at a glance. A well-designed Grafana dashboard provides 'at-a-glance' awareness of network health — the NOC operator can identify problems within seconds. Without visualization, the NOC relies on CLI tools, alerts, and manual checking — which doesn't scale. Grafana is the standard because it's open source, supports virtually any data source, and provides powerful visualization capabilities.
theory.how: Components: 1) Data sources — configure connections to monitoring backends (Prometheus for metrics, Loki for logs, Elasticsearch for logs/inventory). 2) Panels — time series (line graphs), stat panels (single values), gauges (radial dials), heatmaps (distribution over time), bar charts, tables. 3) Dashboards — organize panels into logical views: 'Network Overview', 'Per-Site Status', 'WAN Health', 'Security Events'. 4) Variables — create dropdown filters for dynamic dashboards (select device → show that device's metrics). 5) Annotations — overlay events on graphs (deployments, incidents, changes). 6) Alerting — create alert rules with notification channels. 7) Teams/roles — control dashboard access. Common NOC dashboard structure: top row = overall health (traffic volume, active incidents), left column = site/device selectors, main area = detailed metrics.
theory.when: Create Grafana dashboards for: NOC overview (20,000-foot view of network health), per-site status (detailed metrics for each location), WAN health (utilization, latency, packet loss per circuit), server infrastructure (CPU, memory, disk, network), security monitoring (firewall denied traffic, IDS alerts, VPN tunnels), and capacity planning (growth trends, 95th percentile). Start with a 'NOC Overview' dashboard, then add specialized dashboards per team.
key_concepts: Data sources — Prometheus, InfluxDB, Elasticsearch, CloudWatch, etc.
Panel types — time series, stat, gauge, bar gauge, table, heatmap
Variables — dynamic dashboard filters for devices, sites, metrics
Alert rules — thresholds with notification channels
Annotations — overlay events on graphs (deployments, incidents)
Dashboard JSON — version-controllable, shareable dashboard definition
Loki — Grafana's log aggregation system (correlate metrics + logs)

theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: NOC Overview Dashboard**
Panels:
1. Top row (Stats): Total bandwidth (Gbps), Active alerts count, Sites online/total, Average latency
2. Second row: WAN link utilization graph (all sites overlaid, color-coded)

**Worked Example 2: Correlating Metrics + Logs**

theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• Grafana provides real-time visualization of monitoring data from any data source
• Design dashboards for 'at-a-glance' awareness — identify problems within seconds
• Use variables for dynamic, reusable dashboards
• Overlay annotations to correlate events with metric changes
• Combine metrics (Prometheus) + logs (Loki) for correlated insights
• Dashboard JSON is version-controllable — treat as code

**Best Practice:** Design dashboards from the NOC operator's perspective: top = summary health stats, middle = detailed graphs, bottom = event/alert history. Use color coding consistently (green=ok, red=problem, yellow=warning). Add drill-down links to detailed dashboards. Review dashboard effectiveness quarterly with NOC operators.
troubleshooting: Check data source connectivity — if panels show 'No Data', the data source may be down
Verify PromQL/query syntax — wrong query returns empty results
Check time range — wrong time range may show no data
Test with known values — if a panel shows unexpected values, test the query directly in the data source

theory.what: Prometheus is an open-source monitoring and alerting toolkit originally built at SoundCloud, now a CNCF project. It uses a pull-based architecture: the Prometheus server scrapes metrics from targets (exporters) at regular intervals and stores them in a time-series database. PromQL (Prometheus Query Language) enables powerful aggregation and analysis of metrics. Key components: the Prometheus server (storage + query engine), exporters (expose metrics from various systems), Alertmanager (handle alerts and deduplication), and service discovery (auto-find targets). The pull model simplifies monitoring by not requiring agents to push — the monitoring server initiates all connections.
theory.why: Prometheus has become the standard for modern infrastructure monitoring because: 1) Pull-based — simpler security (NMS connects to targets, not the reverse). 2) Powerful PromQL — aggregations, rate calculations, threshold detection in one language. 3) Multi-dimensional data model — metrics identified by key-value labels (device, interface, type). 4) Efficient storage — up to 40:1 compression. 5) Auto-discovery — integrates with Kubernetes, Consul, EC2, and more. 6) Alertmanager — sophisticated alert routing, grouping, deduplication. 7) Open standard — huge ecosystem of exporters and integrations. For network monitoring, the SNMP exporter allows Prometheus to scrape traditional SNMP devices and expose the data as Prometheus metrics.
theory.how: Prometheus architecture: 1) Targets — defined in prometheus.yml with scrape intervals (default 60s). 2) Exporters — expose metrics at /metrics endpoint (SNMP exporter, node_exporter for servers, blackbox_exporter for probing). 3) Prometheus server — scrapes targets, stores metrics, evaluates alert rules. 4) Alertmanager — receives alerts from Prometheus, deduplicates, groups, and routes to notification channels (Slack, PagerDuty, email). 5) Grafana — queries Prometheus for visualization. SNMP exporter translates SNMP OIDs into Prometheus metrics using generator.yml configuration. This bridges the gap between traditional network devices (SNMP) and modern monitoring (Prometheus).
theory.when: Use Prometheus for: monitoring all infrastructure metrics, especially container/Kubernetes environments (native integration), along with traditional network devices via SNMP exporter. Best for: time-series metrics, not logs (use Loki or Elasticsearch for logs). Good for: alert rule evaluation with flexible thresholds. Not designed for: event data, long-term historical storage (>1 year), or high-cardinality metrics (many unique label combinations).
key_concepts: Pull-based — server scrapes targets, not agent pushes
Exporters — expose metrics as Prometheus format (node_exporter, SNMP exporter, blackbox_exporter)
PromQL — powerful query language for aggregation, rate, prediction
Time-series — (metric_name, labels) → timestamped values
Alertmanager — alert routing, grouping, deduplication, silencing
Service discovery — auto-find targets via Kubernetes, Consul, file-based
SNMP exporter — bridge traditional network devices to Prometheus
theory.configuration:
# prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'network'
    scrape_interval: 60s
    static_configs:
      - targets:
        - 'snmp-exporter:9116'
    params:
      module: [if_mib]  # Cisco interface monitoring
    relabel_configs:
      - source_labels: [__address__]
        target_label: __param_target
      - source_labels: [__param_target]
        target_label: instance
      - target_label: __address__
        replacement: snmp-exporter:9116

  - job_name: 'linux_servers'
    scrape_interval: 30s
    static_configs:
      - targets:
        - 'server1:9100'
        - 'server2:9100'

# Prometheus recording rules for efficiency
groups:
  - name: network_rules
    rules:
      - record: network:link_utilization_ratio
        expr: rate(ifHCInOctets[5m]) * 8 / ifHighSpeed

# Alert rules
groups:
  - name: network_alerts
    rules:
      - alert: LinkUtilizationHigh
        expr: network:link_utilization_ratio > 0.8
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "Link {{ $labels.instance }} utilization > 80%"
theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Monitoring Router Interface Utilization**
1. Install SNMP exporter (snmp_exporter). 2. Configure generator.yml for Cisco interface MIB. 3. Add SNMP exporter as Prometheus target. 4. Query in PromQL:
  # Input bandwidth rate (bps)
  rate(snmp_ifHCInOctets[5m]) * 8
  
  # Interface utilization as percentage
  rate(snmp_ifHCInOctets{instance="192.168.1.1"}[5m]) * 8 / on(instance,ifIndex) ifHighSpeed * 100

5. Create Grafana dashboard with these queries. 6. Set alert when utilization > 80% for 10 minutes.

**Worked Example 2: Blackbox Probing for Latency Monitoring**
blackbox_exporter probes endpoints via HTTP, ICMP, DNS, or TCP. Configure Prometheus to scrape blackbox with module: icmp for latency monitoring:

  - job_name: 'latency_checks'
    metrics_path: /probe
    params:
      module: [icmp]
    static_configs:
      - targets:
        - '8.8.8.8'
        - '1.1.1.1'

PromQL: probe_duration_seconds — query latency to internet endpoints over time. Alert when latency > 50ms for 5 minutes.

**Worked Example 3: Predicting Disk Full**
PromQL prediction function:
  predict_linear(node_filesystem_free_bytes[1w], 86400) < 0

This predicts when disk will be full (86400 seconds = 1 day from now) based on the last week's trend. Set an alert to warn when prediction threshold is crossed.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• Prometheus uses pull-based scraping with a powerful time-series database
• PromQL enables complex aggregations, rate calculations, and predictive alerts
• Exporters bridge traditional devices (SNMP exporter) to Prometheus metrics
• Alertmanager handles alert deduplication, grouping, and routing
• Prometheus + Grafana is the standard open-source monitoring stack
• Auto discovery reduces configuration overhead for large fleets
• SNMP exporter enables monitoring traditional network devices alongside cloud-native infrastructure

**Best Practice:** Use recording rules for frequently used, expensive PromQL queries. Set scrape intervals appropriate for each metric (30s for servers, 60s for network devices). Use service discovery to automatically find targets. Don't use Prometheus for logs — use Loki for logs, Prometheus for metrics. Monitor Prometheus itself: target scrapes, samples ingested, and alert rules evaluated.
troubleshooting: Check target status on Prometheus Targets page — are targets up or down?
Verify exporter running and accessible from Prometheus server
Test PromQL in the Prometheus graph UI before building dashboards
Check Alertmanager status — alerts may be firing but not routed
Watch for high cardinality: metrics with unique label values per scrape can overwhelm storage

theory.what: Zabbix is an enterprise-class, open-source monitoring platform that supports SNMP, agent-based, and agentless monitoring. Unlike Prometheus (pull-based metrics), Zabbix can do active and passive checks, making it more flexible for environments where devices cannot initiate connections. Key components: Zabbix Server (central processing engine), Zabbix Agent (installed on monitored hosts, collects OS/application data), Zabbix Proxy (distributed monitoring for remote locations), Templates (pre-defined monitoring configurations for different device types), Triggers (threshold conditions that generate events), and Actions (notification responses to triggers). Zabbix has built-in graphing, alerting, and reporting — it can function as a complete monitoring solution without additional tools.
theory.why: Zabbix is widely used in enterprise NOCs because: 1) All-in-one — includes data collection, storage, visualization, alerting without needing separate tools. 2) SNMP support — out-of-the-box templates for common devices (Cisco, HP, Dell). 3) Agent-based options — check OS-level metrics (CPU, memory, disk, processes) on Windows/Linux servers. 4) Proxy architecture — deploy Zabbix proxies at remote sites; they buffer data and forward to central server when WAN is up. 5) Built-in reporting — SLA reports, availability reports. 6) Low learning curve compared to Prometheus + Grafana + Alertmanager stack. For small to medium NOCs, Zabbix provides a complete monitoring solution in one package.
theory.how: Zabbix workflow: 1) Install Zabbix Server (database + web interface + server process). 2) Create hosts (devices/servers) with SNMP credentials. 3) Assign templates (pre-configured item + trigger collections for device types). 4) Configure triggers (conditions that generate events, e.g., CPU > 90% for 5 minutes). 5) Configure actions (what happens when trigger fires: email, SMS, Slack notification, script execution). 6) Use auto-discovery to automatically find and add devices (SNMP discovery, network discovery). The Zabbix web interface provides dashboards, graphs, screens, maps, and reports. Zabbix Proxy enables remote monitoring: proxies collect data at remote sites and sync to the central server, resilient to WAN failures.
theory.when: Use Zabbix for: enterprise environments requiring an all-in-one monitoring solution, environments with SNMP-heavy device fleets, organizations that prefer agent-based monitoring where supported, NOCs that need built-in SLA reporting. Use Prometheus instead when: your environment is heavily containerized (Kubernetes), you need PromQL's powerful query language, or you prefer the open-standards ecosystem. Many organizations use both: Zabbix for traditional network monitoring, Prometheus for cloud-native infrastructure.
key_concepts: Templates — pre-built monitoring configurations
Triggers — conditions that generate events
Actions — notification responses to triggers
Auto-discovery — automatically find and add devices
SNMP — monitor network devices without agents
Proxy — distributed monitoring for remote sites
Items — individual data points (CPU, memory, interface utilization)
Host groups — organize devices for management and permissions
theory.configuration:
# Zabbix SNMP item configuration (web UI or API)
Host: Core-SW-01
  SNMP version: v2c
  Community: public
  Templates: Cisco Switch SNMP
  Macros: {$SNMP_COMMUNITY} = public, {$CPU_WARN} = 80

# Auto-discovery rule

  IP range: 10.0.0.0/24
  SNMP community: public
  Check interval: 3600s (1 hour)
  Device uniqueness: {IP} + {SNMP index}
  Actions: Add host, Link Cisco template

# Trigger

  Expression: {Cisco-Switch:system.cpu.util[snmp].avg(5m)} > {$CPU_WARN}

theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Zabbix Proxy for Remote Site Monitoring**
Scenario: Monitoring 10 remote branch offices over MPLS WAN. Each office has 2 routers, 3 switches, and 1 firewall.

Without proxy: Zabbix Server polls all 60 devices directly across the WAN. If WAN goes down, data is lost. Server must reach every device.

With proxy: Deploy a Zabbix Proxy VM at each site. Proxy polls local devices (fast, no WAN latency). Proxy sends summarized data to central server every 60 seconds. If WAN goes down, proxy stores data locally and syncs when WAN recovers. Central server manages all proxies as a single pane of glass.

Result: Resilient monitoring, reduced WAN traffic, single management interface.

**Worked Example 2: Triggering on Complex Conditions**
Trigger: Alert if interface utilization > 90% AND this isn't peak backup time.

Zabbix trigger expression:
  {Switch:ifInOctets.avg(5m)} / {Switch:ifSpeed.last()} * 100 > 90
  AND
  {Zabbix server:timeofday.not_in(22:00-02:00)}

This prevents false alerts during the backup window. The trigger only fires during business hours when utilization crosses 90%.

**Worked Example 3: SLA Reporting**
Zabbix calculates availability per host: uptime / (uptime + downtime) × 100. Generate monthly SLA report for each critical device. Report shows: overall uptime %, total downtime, number of outages, longest outage, MEAN time to repair.

Configure SLA: 99.9% target. SLA status shows green (meeting) or red (breached). Zabbix can send automatic SLA report via email on the first of each month.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• Zabbix is an all-in-one enterprise monitoring platform with SNMP, agent, and proxy support
• Templates provide pre-built monitoring for common device types
• Proxy architecture enables resilient remote site monitoring
• Auto-discovery reduces manual configuration overhead
• Built-in SLA reporting and alerting — no additional tools needed
• Best for traditional network environments with SNMP-heavy device fleets

**Best Practice:** Use templates consistently for standardization. Deploy Zabbix proxies for remote sites. Set up auto-discovery to automatically add new devices. Tune trigger thresholds after the first month of data. Use maintenance windows to suppress alerts during planned work. Review SLA reports monthly.
troubleshooting: Check host availability in Zabbix web UI (ZBX icon = agent, SNMP icon = SNMP)
Verify SNMP community string and version match device configuration
Check proxy connectivity if remote site data is missing
Review trigger configuration for correct expression syntax
For 'Not supported' items: check that the OID exists on the device

theory.what: LibreNMS is an open-source, auto-discovering network monitoring system (fork of the now-defunct Observium). It automatically discovers devices, interfaces, and services using SNMP and provides comprehensive monitoring: interface utilization, CPU/memory, temperature, error rates, wireless metrics, and more. Key features: auto-discovery (finds hosts via SNMP scanning, CDP/LLDP neighbors, and network ranges), alerting (flexible rule-based system), billing (track bandwidth usage per interface or aggregate), API (REST API for integration), distributed polling (multiple pollers for scale), and support for various authentication methods (LDAP, Active Directory, Radius). LibreNMS supports a vast ecosystem of device OS definitions, making it compatible with thousands of device types.
theory.why: LibreNMS is the leading free alternative to commercial NMS products like SolarWinds, PRTG, and What'sUp Gold. Key advantages: 1) Auto-discovery — add a network range and LibreNMS finds everything (devices, interfaces, IPs, neighbors). 2) No per-device licensing — monitor unlimited devices at no additional cost. 3) Active community — frequent updates, 700+ device OS definitions. 4) Rich features — alerting, billing, API, reporting. 5] Integration — can be a data source for Grafana. For organizations with large networks but limited budgets, LibreNMS provides SolarWinds-level monitoring at zero software cost.
theory.how: LibreNMS uses SNMP as the primary data collection protocol. It performs a cycle: auto-discovery (scheduled, e.g., daily) finds new devices, then polling (every 5 minutes by default) collects metrics. The workflow: 1) SNMP scan target network (10.0.0.0/24). 2) Discovered devices are added with OS identification (Cisco IOS, Juniper JUNOS, etc.). 3) Interfaces, IPs, and neighbors are discovered via MIB-II, CDP/LLDP. 4) Metrics collected every 5 minutes: interface utilization, errors, CPU, memory, temperature. 5) Alert rules evaluated after each poll. 6) Data visualized in built-in or Grafana dashboards. Distributed polling allows multiple pollers for large deployments (10,000+ ports), with a central master polling server coordinating via memcached.
theory.when: Use LibreNMS when: you need a free, production-grade NMS; you have a large network (500+ devices) where per-device licensing is expensive; you want auto-discovery to simplify device management; or you need bandwidth billing capabilities. Use a commercial NMS (SolarWinds, PRTG) when: you need vendor support, integrated reporting, or advanced features like NetFlow analysis (though LibreNMS has some NetFlow integration via external tools).
key_concepts: Auto-discovery — finds devices via SNMP, CDP/LLDP, or network scanning
SNMP polling — collects metrics every 5 minutes
Alerting — rule-based alert system with transport options (email, Slack, API)
Billing — track bandwidth per port, aggregate, or customer
API — REST API for third-party integration and automation
Distributed polling — multiple pollers for large-scale deployments
Device OS definitions — YAML-based definitions for device support

theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: Auto-Discovering a New Office**
New remote office is built. Switch and router installed, connected to network. LibreNMS auto-discovery runs daily:

1. LibreNMS scans 192.168.10.0/24 (the new office subnet).
2. Finds router at 192.168.10.1, switch at 192.168.10.2.
3. Discover device OS: router = 'ios', switch = 'ios'.
4. Discover interfaces: GigabitEthernet0/0 (WAN), GigabitEthernet0/1-48 (access).
5. Discover IPs and MACs on each interface.
6. Discover CDP/LLDP neighbors: connected to upstream switch 'Core-SW-01'.
7. Start polling: interface utilization, CPU, memory, temperature.
8. Alerts configured via template: if any interface goes down, alert.

No manual intervention required. The new office is automatically monitored.

**Worked Example 2: Bandwidth Billing**
LibreNMS billing feature tracks bandwidth per customer or per interface. Create a bill: 'Customer ABC — primary internet link'. Define the bill by interface GigabitEthernet0/1 on the edge router. Set bandwidth limit: 100 Mbps. LibreNMS tracks inbound/outbound traffic and calculates monthly usage. At end of month: 'Customer ABC used 2.5 TB of 3.3 TB available (75% of 100 Mbps port).' Generate bill PDF or export via API.

**Worked Example 3: Using LibreNMS with Grafana**
LibreNMS stores data in RRD files (Round Robin Database). To use Grafana: 1) Configure LibreNMS to also write to InfluxDB (or Prometheus with snmp_exporter). 2) Add InfluxDB as data source in Grafana. 3) Create Grafana dashboards with LibreNMS data. 4) Use LibreNMS for alerting (native notification system), Grafana for visualization (more flexible than LibreNMS built-in graphs).

Alternatively: use the InfluxDB-reporter or Prometheus connector in LibreNMS to forward metrics.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• LibreNMS is a free, auto-discovering NMS with SolarWinds-class capabilities
• Auto-discovery finds devices via SNMP scanning, CDP/LLDP, and network ranges
• Supports unlimited devices at no licensing cost
• Built-in alerting, billing, and API for integration
• Integrates with Grafana for advanced visualization
• Distributed polling scales to 10,000+ devices
• 700+ device OS definitions provide broad vendor support

**Best Practice:** Use auto-discovery with network scanning to ensure no devices are missed. Regularly update LibreNMS for new device OS definitions. Configure alert rules for all critical infrastructure. Use LibreNMS as the authoritative device inventory (auto-discovery maintains it). Integrate with Grafana for enhanced visualization.
troubleshooting: Check device polling status in LibreNMS web UI (green = ok, red = unreachable)
Verify SNMP access to device (snmpwalk from LibreNMS server)
Check discovery and poller logs if devices not appearing
Verify SNMP community string or v3 credentials match device configuration
For performance issues: verify polling time; if > 300 seconds, enable distributed polling

theory.what: NetBox is an open-source application for IP address management (IPAM) and data center infrastructure management (DCIM), originally developed by DigitalOcean. It serves as a 'source of truth' for network documentation — a single, authoritative database of everything in the network: IP addresses, VLANs, VRFs, devices (with rack positions, serial numbers, asset tags), circuits (carriers, circuit IDs, bandwidth), cables (physical connectivity), power connections, and more. NetBox is API-first — every object can be created, read, updated, or deleted via REST API, enabling full automation integration. It uses a plugin system for extensibility and supports custom fields, tags, and webhooks for integrations.
theory.why: Without a single source of truth, IP conflicts become common (two engineers assign the same IP to different devices), device inventory becomes scattered across spreadsheets (which are never updated), and cable management becomes impossible. NetBox solves these by: 1) Preventing IP conflicts — the database won't let you assign an IP that's already in use. 2) Tracking every device with its model, serial, warranty, and location. 3) Documenting cable connections — trace a cable from switch port to patch panel to server NIC. 4) Recording circuits — carrier contacts, circuit IDs, bandwidth, contract dates. 5) Providing a complete API — automation tools query NetBox for the 'ground truth' about the network. NetBox becomes the foundation of all network operations: configuration management tools (Ansible, NAPALM) reference NetBox for device info, change management references NetBox for impact analysis, and NOC engineers reference NetBox for troubleshooting.
theory.how: NetBox data model: Sites (physical locations) → Racks (equipment racks in sites) → Devices (installed in racks with positions and faces) → Interfaces (device ports) → Cable connections (interface-to-interface connections). IPAM: VRFs (virtual routing and forwarding) → Prefixes/Subnets (IP ranges) → IP Addresses (individual assignments to interfaces). Circuits: Providers (carriers) → Circuit types (fiber, MPLS, broadband) → Circuits (with circuit IDs, bandwidth, contract info). VLANs: VLAN groups → VLANs → VLAN-to-device assignment. Power: Power panels → Power feeds → Power connections. NetBox supports custom fields for data not covered by built-in models (e.g., 'OS version', 'Contract renewal date').
theory.when: Use NetBox as the authoritative source for: 1) IPAM — tracking all IP assignments, preventing conflicts, managing subnets. 2) Device inventory — knowing what you have, where it is, and its status. 3) DCIM — tracking rack space, power, and cabling. 4) Circuit management — tracking carrier connections, contracts, and bandwidth. 5) Automation integration — Ansible/Terraform read from NetBox API for device configuration. NetBox is the foundation of Network Automation — you can't automate what you haven't documented.
key_concepts: IPAM — IP address management, prefix hierarchy, conflict prevention
DCIM — data center infrastructure management (racks, devices, cables)
Source of truth — single, authoritative database for all network info
API-first — all operations available via REST API
Custom fields — extend the data model for organization-specific data
Webhooks — event-driven integrations with external systems
Labels and tags — organize objects for filtering and reporting
VLAN/VRF management — complete Layer 2/Layer 3 addressing control

theory.worked_examples:
**Worked Example 1: IP Conflict Prevention**
Situation: Two engineers need to assign IPs for new servers.

Before NetBox: Engineer A assigns 10.0.0.50/24 from memory. Engineer B also assigns 10.0.0.50/24 to a different server. The second server can't communicate — IP conflict. Investigation takes 30 minutes.

With NetBox: Engineer A creates the IP in NetBox. When Engineer B tries to create the same IP, NetBox rejects it with 'This IP address already exists.' Engineer B sees the IP is in use and picks 10.0.0.51 instead. Zero conflict, zero investigation time.

**Worked Example 2: Disaster Recovery with NetBox**
Scenario: A P1 incident destroys the primary data center. You need to rebuild in a DR site.

With NetBox: Export complete device list (100s of devices), IP assignments per device, VLAN configurations, circuit information, and cable connections. NetBox data populates the DR site network design within hours. You know exactly what equipment you need, how it was connected, and what IP addresses were in use.

Without NetBox: Start from memory, scattered spreadsheets, and sticky notes. Rebuild would take weeks and would be incomplete.

**Worked Example 3: Automation Integration**
CI/CD pipeline queries NetBox for device information:
1. Ansible playbook reads inventory from NetBox API.
2. Ansible uses device OS (from NetBox) to select the right module (ios_config, junos_config).
3. Ansible applies configuration template with IP addresses from NetBox.
4. After change, Ansible updates NetBox with new config version.
5. Oxidized backs up running config and stores it alongside NetBox device record.

Cable management: An engineer traces a cable from server eth0 → Patch panel 12-A → Switch Gi1/0/5 by following NetBox cable connections. Clear documentation of the physical path enables faster troubleshooting and moves/adds/changes.
theory.summary:
**Key Takeaways:**
• NetBox is the single source of truth for IPAM, device inventory, and DCIM
• API-first design enables full automation integration
• IP conflict prevention — database won't allow duplicate assignments
• Cable management — trace physical connectivity end-to-end
• Circuits management — track carriers, contract, bandwidth
• Crucial for disaster recovery — complete network documentation in one place
• Foundation for automation — Ansible/Terraform reference NetBox as source of truth

**Best Practice:** Maintain NetBox as the authoritative source. All IP assignments must go through NetBox. Update NetBox at the time of change, not after. Integrate NetBox with monitoring (LibreNMS/Zabbix) for auto-population of device inventory. Full API documentation available at /api/docs/.
troubleshooting: Check IP conflicts by searching NetBox for the conflicting address
Verify device records in NetBox before starting troubleshooting
Review VLAN assignments in NetBox when troubleshooting connectivity between devices
Check cable connections in NetBox to verify physical connectivity
Use webhooks for real-time notifications when devices or IPs change
